Chinatown is a beautifully made and highly respected neo-noir mystery, but personally, it didn't work for me. The film follows private detective J.J. “Jake” Gittes as he investigates what initially appears to be a simple case involving a wealthy Los Angeles family. The mystery gradually becomes much darker and more complicated. There is no doubt that the filmmaking is excellent. Roman Polanski creates a fantastic noir atmosphere, the cinematography is beautiful, and Robert Towne's screenplay is considered one of the great screenplays of American cinema. Jack Nicholson is also excellent as Jake Gittes. His performance has plenty of charm and personality, and he fits the private-detective role perfectly. Faye Dunaway is also strong, particularly as the mystery surrounding Evelyn Mulwray becomes increasingly complicated. But despite all that... I was bored. 😭 The pacing is simply too slow for my taste. The investigation takes a long time to develop, and many of the conversations and discoveries didn't keep me interested enough. The mystery itself is complicated, but for me, complicated didn't necessarily mean engaging. There were moments where I was more interested in seeing the movie finish than finding out what happened. The film's atmosphere is impressive, but atmosphere alone isn't enough to make me enjoy a movie. The story also becomes increasingly dark and disturbing, especially towards the end. I can appreciate what the filmmakers were trying to achieve, but emotionally I never connected with it. The ending is undeniably powerful and tragic, and I understand why it is so highly regarded. But again, respecting a film and enjoying a film are two different things. Chinatown clearly has enormous influence and technical quality. It simply isn't my kind of movie. Overall, Chinatown is a technically brilliant and historically important neo-noir, elevated by Jack Nicholson, Faye Dunaway and an excellent screenplay, but its slow pacing and style made it a boring and unenjoyable experience for me. A great film for many people — just absolutely not my cup of tea. 🖤🎬

Chinatown can be filed under the category of "beloved movie classics that Ditzy doesn't care about". I really tried with this one. I did some additional research, I sat with it for 5+ hours, I mulled it and... eh. I can enjoy a good noir movie from time to time but Chinatown didn't blow me away or even really interest me that much. The movie follows PI Jack Nicholson who stumbles into a plot involving the Los Angeles drought. Someone is needlessly dumping of reservoir water, secretly buying enormous swaths of land and killing anyone who gets too close to the truth. Nicholson finds himself working with rich widow who has many secrets and close ties to the conspiracy. It's a twisty rabbit hole that ends on a bleak, nigh hopeless note. The finale is one of the few things in the film that I like; it was deliciously macabre and a great twist of the knife. As the film went on, it became increasingly clear that there would be no sound resolution and the climax struck that chord masterfully. I also found that Jack Nicholson worked very well as the protagonist; equal parts sleaze, sass, charm and cunning.  Nicholson truly was one of the great performers of our time and may he rest in peace. I'm not sure if he was in any other noir features but he did very well with this material. He's just tortured, moody and curious enough to sell it as a sleuth. I liked the ending and Nicholson but everything else... meh. I found the Faye Dunaway character to be infuriating. She implicated herself in the conspiracy so many times just to protect the family secrets. I get that they were going for the challenging femme fatale with her but she was infuriating in her self sabotage. I also couldn't stand how pathetic she was; far too passive given the circumstances. There was also a scene where Nicholson had to slap the truth out of her and that... sucked. I found the conspiracy in Chinatown to be super underwhelming. There wasn't much of a surprise either; just your usual, crazy, capitalist land development bullshit. "Once I contrive a water shortage and buy up valley property, I will incorporate the rural land into the city and develop it for profit! Mwahaha!" Alrighty then... so glad I waited two hours for that. Chinatown has some style and intrigue but it's also boring. It also didn't have much to say when the chips were down. I was made to anticipate a super engaging, advanced, heart-wrenching story but what I found was just... Chinatown. I was optimistic going in because I really enjoyed Roman Polanski's horror classic, Rosemary's Baby. This did not blow me away, though and I doubt I will find myself thinking back on it much in the days and weeks to come. Two Mutzies and salted grass

Good noir: Intellectually great, emotionally distant This was my first time watching Chinatown, and honestly, the thing that pulled me in the most wasn't the mystery, it was the vibe. The world-building is incredible: the clothes, the cars, the quiet jazz, the heat of 1930s Los Angeles, the backyard scenes, the hats, all of it. Jack Nicholson has this classy, effortless presence, and the film's whole aesthetic feels timeless. Great performance by Faye Dunaway too. But the movie itself is emotionally cold. It's a slow burn, and for most of the runtime, I felt like the film kept a distance from me. The message and themes are definitely strong, but for me, they don't fully hit until the final scene, and that's where I had a mixed reaction. It almost feels like the entire movie was built for that final moment, where everything becomes very obviously "noir" and you see the system's corruption laid out. But the thing is: even without that last scene, I already sensed the corruption throughout the film. It's implicit. It's in the world, the tone, the dialogue. So the movie didn't need to rely so heavily on that final punch for me to understand what it was doing. And maybe that's because we watch the film from a third-person perspective. We see signs of the system's rot throughout the story, long before the main character truly realizes it. If I were in the detective's shoes -if I were seeing things only through his head- it would probably feel more engaging and shocking step by step. But as viewers, we catch the overall darkness earlier, which made the ending feel powerful but also slightly predictable in feeling, even if not in plot. So overall, I loved the atmosphere and the classic detective tone, but emotionally it didn't grip me the same way other classics do. Chinatown doesn't grip emotionally at all. It's more observational. More philosophical. You're meant to watch the world and its corruption, not get pulled into the characters' inner lives.

On my recent movie arc, a natural fulcrum point that you reach is whether the classics are worth visiting. Are you watching them because you'll think you'll like them or because movie buffs say you should like them so you HAVE to watch them? I've never been a huge fan of classical acting, a bane that plagues me with movies from the 40s all the way to the 80s. The style is very different and while understandable and appeals to some, I usually find it to date movies too much, it's dramatic in a more theatrical way. As ironic as it sounds I prefer movies that are a little less theatrical with their character portrayals. I prefer more realistic/grounded performances you find in modern acting or performances that are less like caricatures and more like the person they're supposed to be. But times were different, in bygone times of film-making people weren't looking for relatable they were looking for better versions of themselves. A detective that always has the perfect quip, a damsel in distress that is beautiful but sassy but also mysterious!? While I say all of that, I can't help but notice the bright spots in older movies that shine through every time I watch them. Old movies are time capsules of the past that allow you to see the origins of where the modern films you love came from; their humble beginnings. With little experience with Noir films of the 40s, 50s and 60s its easy for me to overlook just exactly HOW revolutionary this movie was for the genre at the time of its release. How purposefully theatrical the acting was and how much it used plot devices from these films and then subverted them or expanded upon them. Looking at it through that lens, everything started to click for me, and the biggest thing I noticed is that Jake Gittes isn't the typical noir detective he's actually a flawed man that fails to see the dark corners of the world and our "femme fatale" is actually a traumatized woman and a victim of those same dark corners. This movie is THE quintessential Noir film for me. It wears the influences of its predecessors on its sleeve while also influencing decades of films to follow. While carrying out the tropes you typically see in these movies, it, at least at the time, had an ending that made stomachs churn in defeat at the hopelessness that it leaves you with.  I can confirm that never having been spoiled, for me it had the same effect. It follows an intriguing mystery, that at parts is cliche but also provides nuance in strange places. The acting is great, despite my biases towards modern acting (it took me some getting used to). The shots were innovative for the time and its layered with thick metaphors to the corrupt vs life on the surface throughout. AND nearly every scene has a double-meaning or a callback for later. I was thoroughly engaged and it accomplished what I hope to see in any watching of a classic movie according to critics. It MADE SENSE why this movie was influential and considered a classic. Has the formula been improved upon since this film? Probably. Is it dated and completely different from a Noir film that would be made today? Yes.... I mean, noir as a genre itself is dated. BUT! Did I enjoy myself with this film? HELL YEAH! That's all I can ask for, and in my surprise of how much I enjoyed this movie I sometimes caught myself stopping to appreciate what it did at the time it came out. The fact that i'm a big Jack Nicholson fan also helped a tremendous amount.

Chinatown é um clássico absoluto do cinema, e ao assisti-lo você entende bem o porquê. Roman Polanski é extremamente feliz ao retratar a Los Angeles da década de 30, nos trazendo uma ambientação impecável e visuais que transcendem as décadas. A trama acompanha J.J. Gittes, um detetive particular de Los Angeles, interpretado de forma majestosa por Jack Nicholson, que investiga e resolve pequenas intrigas na cidade. No entanto, as coisas mudam para o seu lado quando uma mulher misteriosa aparece com uma proposta para ele. O roteiro de Robert Towne, somado à direção de Roman Polanski, traz um forte aspecto de investigação noir que deixa o filme cada vez mais imersivo. Gittes vai se enfiando cada vez mais fundo na cidade, e percebemos, a cada passo que ele dá, que as coisas não são tão simples quanto imaginamos. O roteiro não deixa pontas soltas, sempre trazendo à tona pistas deixadas durante a trama, que cada vez mais parece um rio sem fundo. Polanski é muito inventivo, mostrando como pode causar tensão, angústia, medo apenas pela forma como ele traz à tona seus personagens. Isto pode ser visto de forma clara em cenas em que Gittes tem que dialogar e obter informações de diferentes pessoas, com destaque para um plano anterior a um diálogo no carro, no qual Polanski constrói o clima da cena antes mesmo dela acontecer. Essa definitivamente é uma obra que agradaria a gregos e troianos. Mais um para a lista da faculdade 🎥

I'm on a big noir kick at the moment, and finally getting to watch this detective masterpiece just feels SO good. Last year, I read The Big Sleep, then watched the Humphrey Bogart movie and loved it. Chinatown blows The Big Sleep right out of the water, putting it to its own big sleep (death). There is so much to appreciate in this movie, and we of course have to acknowledge how fucked up Roman Polanski is as a human being. That's the shadow that looms over not only this movie, but Polanski's long and storied filmography. Unfortunately, given how well-made this movie is, I can only imagine I'll be dipping my toes back in soon enough. Before this, I'd only seen Rosemary's Baby, which is also great, but in a very different genre. Chinatown fully nails the detective noir feel without the darkness and rain that's always associated with it. It's crazy that pretty much all of this is filmed during the daytime, showing off Los Angeles from the 70's. I've only been to LA once, but this feels like a quintessential LA film. It's like a moment in time, interestingly enough depicting what I THINK is the 30's here. So it's like a double snapshot. Very cool. Young Jack Nicholson as Jake Gittes is a perfect noir detective. He's got all the charm, charisma, and acting talent that it requires, while also just giving that superstar quality. My experience with Young Nicholson is pretty much only in The Shining, so getting to see him really SHINE here was a delight. He's got the look down, rocking the shit out of that suit that gets more and more fucked up as the movie goes on. He's got the line deliveries that I could read right off the page. There are way too many to count, but I found myself smiling at the end of each of his conversations because they almost always end with a witty, killer noir line of dialogue. Plus, we get some really cool and smart detective work, which I'll always be a fan of. Specifically, when Nicholson tracks a car's movement by placing a stopwatch under the wheel and then checking when the watch is busted. I love stuff like that, and it gives us a glimpse into the strategies of detectives nearly a hundred years ago. Yes, the mystery is a LITTLE convoluted, but not overly so. I was able to mostly understand what was going on, and the credit there goes to the writing. It's a great script, consistently teasing new information that changes everyone's perspectives as the mystery grows in scope. Then, that mystery becomes a tragedy with horrific implications, leading to a truly shocking ending. It's bleak but done in a VERY profound way. The conclusion here will stick with me for a long time. But ironically, the story is weirdly prophetic to 2026. Corruption is everywhere, and those corrupt people are wealthy criminals stealing water from those who need it, STRANGELY SIMILAR to what's going on now with Data Centers and the rich bastards behind them who don't actually care about helping human beings. It's all about greed, in the end, in this movie NAILS that concept. It's crazy and incredibly frustrating how much this parallels today's world. It starts with just stealing water, but then what? I guess we'll see. The music is exactly what I was hoping for. Soft trumpet melodies that only pop up in certain points of the runtime, which I think works really well. It doesn't overpower, but I was SO excited every time that trumpet kicked in. It works super well at giving us that classic noir vibe. Something I don't often notice (likely on purpose) is the LIGHTING in a movie, but there are some jaw dropping moments of really interesting lighting choices. The standout is the final conversation between Nicholson and Dunaway in the car, where each sets of eyes are isolated by the lighting. The look is fascinating and helps show the possibilities of what lighting can do. The villain, eventually revealed, is a true and unfortunately very believable bad guy (again, with plenty of modern-day parallels). I won't spoil anything but just know that you'll be infuriated by this character. So smarmy and gross, but also powerful and scary. To come back to the ending, it's a powerful choice that feels depressing in a way that should anger viewers, not because of the choice itself, but because of the implications of it. I was shocked by every single twist, including the big one in the final third that fully changes your perspective on everything you've seen before. Finally watching Chinatown has inspired me to want to try my hand at a detective story sometime soon. It's just such a fun genre with great characters and dialogue, that I feel like I have to give it a shot. I would never do this, but this movie could be remade now in 2026 and still have a lot of the same ideas. That alone shows the staying power it has. I could very much see myself watching this again down the road, either for inspiration or entertainment. It's a classic for a reason, and now I'll have to go check out some more Polanski movies. But also, fuck that coward.

THE TRUTH WAS NEVER ENOUGH. Chinatown è uno di quei noir che riescono a essere molto più di un semplice mistero da risolvere. Polanski parte da una storia apparentemente classica, fatta di tradimenti, ricatti e segreti, e costruisce lentamente un mondo in cui ogni risposta apre una porta su qualcosa di molto più grande. Jake Gittes è un detective convinto di sapere come muoversi in quel mondo. È intelligente, sicuro di sé e abituato a pensare di poter arrivare alla verità prima degli altri. Ma più si addentra nella vicenda, più si accorge che non tutto può essere controllato. Dietro il caso ci sono il potere, il denaro, l’acqua e una Los Angeles che sotto la sua superficie luminosa nasconde una realtà molto più sporca. E forse è proprio qui che il film mi ha convinto di più. Gittes non è l’eroe che arriva, risolve il caso e rimette tutto al proprio posto. Fa quello che può, arriva alla verità e prova persino a cambiare il destino di Evelyn. Ma conoscere la verità non significa necessariamente avere il potere di cambiarla. Il finale, per questo, è devastante proprio nella sua semplicità. Non cancella ciò che Gittes ha scoperto: gli mostra semplicemente quanto poco possa bastare, a volte, per fermare qualcosa che è ormai molto più grande di lui. “Forget it, Jake. It’s Chinatown.” Un noir elegantissimo e amarissimo, costruito con una precisione quasi perfetta e capace di lasciare addosso quella rara sensazione di aver assistito a una tragedia che, una volta iniziata, forse non poteva più avere un finale diverso.

El estreno de Chinatown en 1974 no sólo consagró a Roman Polanski, Jack Nicholson y Robert Towne, sino que transformó para siempre el cine policíaco. Es una de esas películas en las que todo parece ocupar exactamente el lugar que debe: el guion, los personajes, la fotografía, la música, la ambientación y, sobre todo, una concepción del mundo profundamente pesimista. No es casualidad que apareciera precisamente en 1974. Estados Unidos atravesaba una profunda crisis de confianza en sus instituciones. Watergate acababa de llevar a Nixon a la dimisión y Vietnam había dejado una enorme sensación de fracaso y desengaño. Chinatown recoge ese clima y lo convierte en ficción: aquí la corrupción no se encuentra en los bajos fondos, sino en las estructuras mismas del poder. Noah Cross no es simplemente un criminal; es un hombre integrado en el sistema, rico, respetado y prácticamente intocable. La película pertenece además, de lleno al Nuevo Hollywood, aquel cine de los setenta que empezó a desconfiar de los finales tranquilizadores y de la justicia poética. Y pocas películas llevaron esa desconfianza tan lejos. Jake Gittes investiga porque cree que, como detective, descubrir la verdad significa acercarse a una solución. Pero cada respuesta sólo abre una nueva puerta hacia algo peor. Su investigación no consigue restablecer el orden: consigue demostrar que el orden ya estaba podrido. El guión de Robert Towne es extraordinario precisamente por esa manera de hacer crecer el misterio. Lo que comienza como un caso aparentemente relacionado con la gestión del agua de Los Ángeles termina conectando corrupción política, intereses económicos y una tragedia familiar monstruosa. La investigación funciona simultáneamente como thriller y como descenso moral: cuanto más sabe Jake, menos capaz es de controlar las consecuencias de aquello que descubre. Y Polanski entiende perfectamente que ese mundo debe estar filmado bajo una luz completamente distinta a la del noir clásico. Chinatown utiliza el color, el Panavision y el sol abrasador de Los Ángeles para construir un auténtico noir a plena luz del día. No necesitamos callejones oscuros ni lluvia para encontrar la podredumbre. Está delante de nosotros, perfectamente iluminada, escondida detrás de mansiones, oficinas, piscinas y hombres respetables. Jack Nicholson está magnífico como Jake Gittes. Su detective conserva el cinismo, el ingenio y la arrogancia del protagonista clásico, pero Polanski le quita la seguridad de saber que al final podrá arreglar las cosas. Jake puede descubrir la verdad, pero no puede controlar el mundo en el que esa verdad existe. Y ahí está una de las grandes diferencias con el detective del cine negro tradicional: no fracasa porque no haya sido suficientemente inteligente, sino porque se enfrenta a un poder que está fuera de su alcance. Faye Dunaway convierte a Evelyn Mulwray en algo mucho más complejo que una femme fatale convencional. Parece inicialmente sospechosa, pero poco a poco comprendemos que ella también es una víctima. El verdadero poder no está en la mujer misteriosa que oculta secretos, sino en el hombre que posee los recursos para decidir qué secretos pueden salir a la luz y cuáles permanecerán enterrados. Y entonces llega ese final. Polanski decidió mantener un desenlace mucho más cruel que el que originalmente imaginaba Towne, y la decisión resulta fundamental para la película. Evelyn muere, Cross consigue lo que quiere y Jake sólo puede contemplar cómo todo aquello que había intentado evitar sucede delante de él. La investigación ha sido correcta; sus conclusiones también. Lo que resulta inútil es pensar que conocer la verdad basta para que exista justicia. “Olvídalo, Jake. Es Chinatown.” Pocas frases resumen con tanta precisión una película. Chinatown no es únicamente un lugar: es una forma de entender el mundo. Un territorio donde las buenas intenciones, la inteligencia y el esfuerzo individual pueden resultar completamente insuficientes frente a estructuras de poder mucho más grandes. Por eso considero que Chinatown no sólo es una obra maestra del cine negro, sino una de las grandes películas sobre la impotencia del individuo frente al poder. Toma todos los elementos del noir clásico —el detective privado, la mujer misteriosa, la corrupción, la investigación, la ciudad— y los conserva para después destruir las expectativas que llevaban asociadas. El detective no salva a nadie. La víctima no obtiene justicia. El culpable no recibe su castigo. Y descubrir la verdad no cambia absolutamente nada. Ese pesimismo, unido a una puesta en escena de una precisión extraordinaria, convierte Chinatown en una película prácticamente perfecta. Un misterio criminal que termina siendo algo mucho más oscuro: el descubrimiento de que, en determinados lugares, la verdad puede ser perfectamente conocida y seguir siendo completamente inútil.

Era uno de los grandes clásicos del cine negro que todavía tenía pendiente de ver, y la verdad es que no me ha decepcionado. Roman Polanski hace un trabajazo en la dirección. Me gusta mucho cómo va construyendo la historia poco a poco, haciendo que el misterio vaya creciendo a medida que avanza la película. Además, los planos y la puesta en escena ayudan muchísimo a crear esa sensación de tensión e incomodidad que está presente durante prácticamente toda la película. La ambientación de Los Ángeles de los años 30 también me parece increíble y le da a la película una personalidad enorme. La interpretación de Jack Nicholson es sobresaliente. Su personaje, Jake. J. Gittes, tiene muchísimo carisma, pero también es bastante cínico y arrogante, y creo que Nicholson consigue transmitir muy bien todas esas facetas. Si no me equivoco, este fue uno de sus primeros papeles realmente importantes en Hollywood, y demostró que podía llevar perfectamente el peso de una película. Y ese final... Uff. Creo que es casi lo mejor de la película. Me parece un cierre brutal, tanto por lo que ocurre como por la forma en la que está planteado. Es de esos finales que hacen que, cuando terminan los créditos, te quedes unos minutos pensando en lo que acabas de ver. Lo dicho, creo que Chinatown es una de las mejores películas policíacas y de cine negro que he visto. Tiene una historia muy bien construida, una atmósfera increíble y un final difícil de olvidar. Una auténtica joya que recomiendo muchísimo. 👌
